approaches.name: Pediatric direct lateral approach to the femoral shaft
approaches.corridor: Longitudinal fascia-lata opening followed by anterior extraperiosteal elevation of vastus lateralis from the lateral intermuscular septum and linea aspera

sources.title: Comparison of submuscular and open plating of pediatric femur fractures: a retrospective review
Pediatric Femoral Shaft Fractures: A Multicenter Review of the AAOS Clinical Practice Guidelines Before and After 2009

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric femoral-shaft fracture requires direct reduction, debridement, grafting, or open plate application rather than closed nailing or submuscular bridge plating

positioning.text: Position supine with a bolster under the ipsilateral hip or lateral, keeping the full femur accessible and imageable from hip to knee.

setup.text: Plan the minimum exposure necessary, plate position and length, reduction method, and blood-loss response before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the greater trochanter, lateral femoral epicondyle, shaft axis, fracture level, and planned plate extent.

incision.text: Incise longitudinally on the lateral thigh along the line between the greater trochanter and lateral epicondyle, with length determined by the fracture and fixation objective.

superficial_interval.text: Open fascia lata parallel to its fibers, bluntly separate vastus lateralis from fascia, and retract the muscle anteromedially.

deep_interval.text: Incise vastus lateralis fascia 1 cm anterior to the lateral intermuscular septum and elevate the muscle extraperiosteally from the septum and linea aspera.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, vastus lateralis fascia, extraperiosteal plane along the lateral intermuscular septum, then lateral femoral cortex.

structures_encountered.text: Fascia lata, vastus lateralis, lateral intermuscular septum, linea aspera, perforating vessels, periosteum, and lateral shaft are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Profunda femoris perforators are the primary structures at risk; the major vessels and nerves remain medial or posteromedial when the dissection stays lateral.

danger_zones.text: Identify and protect or ligate perforators before division because their proximal ends can retract through the septum and cause troublesome occult posterior-compartment bleeding.

retraction_hazards.text: Keep retractors directly on bone and avoid deep medial or posterior passage, circumferential stripping, and prolonged forceful anterior retraction of vastus lateralis.

exposure.text: Provides extensile direct access to the lateral shaft for reduction, debridement, grafting, and plate fixation.

limitations.text: Compared with submuscular plating, open exposure increases blood loss and disrupts more muscle and fracture biology, so exposure should be limited to the operative need.

extensions.text: Extend distally along the shaft; proximally release vastus lateralis origin in an L shape through the interval between gluteus medius and vastus lateralis.

indications.text: Use when direct visualization is required for an irreducible fracture, open injury, debridement, interposed tissue, grafting, or compression plating.

relative_contraindications.text: Favor closed nailing or submuscular plating when adequate alignment and stability can be achieved without exposing the fracture and when lateral soft tissues are compromised.

implant_implications.text: Choose plate length and screw pattern for compression versus bridge mechanics, avoid trapping muscle under the plate, and preserve periosteal attachments outside the required reduction zone.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm length, alignment, rotation, plate position, screw length, and hip and knee orientation despite direct visualization of the fracture.

closure.text: Secure perforator hemostasis, return vastus lateralis over the femur, repair any proximal origin release and fascia lata, then close subcutaneous tissue and skin.

complications.text: Complications include occult perforator bleeding, hematoma or compartment syndrome, muscle devascularization, infection, malrotation, limb-length discrepancy, nonunion, implant failure, and stiffness.

bailouts.text: For uncontrolled bleeding, stop blind clamping, enlarge the exposure and control the retracted perforator directly; convert reduction or fixation strategy when biology or alignment is being compromised.

questions.question: Where is vastus lateralis fascia incised?
questions.answer: One centimeter anterior to the lateral intermuscular septum.

questions.question: Which vessels require deliberate control?
questions.answer: The profunda femoris perforating bundles crossing from posterior to anterior.

questions.question: Why can bleeding be occult?
questions.answer: A divided proximal perforator can retract through the septum into the posterior compartment.

approaches.name: Pediatric minimally invasive submuscular approach to the femoral shaft
approaches.corridor: Short lateral proximal, shaft, or distal windows connected by an extraperiosteal tunnel deep to vastus lateralis for biologic bridge-plate insertion

sources.title: Submuscular bridge plating for complex pediatric femur fractures is reliable
Submuscular Plate for Pediatric Femoral Fractures

procedure_applications.condition: A pediatric length-unstable, proximal-third, distal-third, or otherwise complex shaft fracture is selected for indirect reduction and submuscular bridge plating

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with an ipsilateral hip bump and unobstructed imaging of the entire femur.

setup.text: Template a long plate and fixation segments, select the proximal or distal main window by fracture location, and obtain indirect length, alignment, and rotation before tunneling.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the greater trochanter, lateral epicondyle, joint line, femoral axis, fracture zone, physes, and planned terminal fixation windows.

incision.text: Use a short lateral incision at the proximal or distal plate end, adding stab incisions for screws and a second limited window only when manipulation requires it.

superficial_interval.text: Split fascia lata longitudinally and open vastus lateralis fascia only within the selected windows; use blunt muscle spreading at midshaft.

deep_interval.text: Elevate vastus lateralis just enough to create an extraperiosteal submuscular tunnel, keeping the plate on the lateral cortex and the fracture envelope intact.

layers.text: Skin windows, subcutaneous tissue, fascia lata, limited vastus lateralis fascia or muscle split, extraperiosteal plane, then lateral femoral cortex.

structures_encountered.text: Vastus lateralis origin and belly, fascia lata, lateral cortex, distal metaphysis, periosteum, and profunda perforators define the working corridor.

structures_at_risk.text: Profunda perforators, major medial vessels, sciatic nerve posteriorly, quadriceps vascularity, physes, and the fracture hematoma are at risk during tunneling and percutaneous drilling.

danger_zones.text: Keep the plate and instruments against lateral cortex; posterior or medial passage and uncontrolled far-cortex drilling threaten neurovascular structures, while physeal crossing risks growth disturbance.

retraction_hazards.text: Use anterior and posterior extraperiosteal Hohmann retractors directly on bone through a visible window and avoid circumferential stripping or blind posterior placement.

exposure.text: Provides terminal fixation access while preserving muscle attachment, periosteal perfusion, fracture hematoma, and comminuted intermediate fragments.

limitations.text: Indirect visualization makes rotation and sagittal alignment vulnerable to error and may require additional windows when reduction or plate position cannot be proven.

extensions.text: For proximal access, release vastus lateralis origin in an extraperiosteal L shape; for distal access, extend toward the lateral epicondyle; add a targeted shaft window only as necessary.

indications.text: Use for unstable, comminuted, proximal-third, or distal-third pediatric femoral fractures where flexible nails may not reliably maintain length and alignment.

relative_contraindications.text: Use open exposure when contamination needs debridement, vascular exploration or direct reduction is required, or acceptable indirect alignment cannot be achieved.

implant_implications.text: Select a long bridge plate spanning the fracture with adequate proximal and distal fixation, appropriate working length, and restrained screw density rather than a short rigid construct.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Repeatedly confirm hip and knee orientation, length, coronal and sagittal alignment, rotation, physeal clearance, plate centering, and screw length.

closure.text: Release retractors, verify hemostasis, allow vastus lateralis to cover the plate, repair any proximal origin release and fascia lata, and close skin.

complications.text: Complications include malrotation, angular or length malalignment, physeal injury, neurovascular injury, infection, delayed union, implant failure, refracture after removal, and stiffness.

bailouts.text: If alignment or plate passage is uncertain, stop blind advancement, add a targeted reduction window or temporary aid, and convert to open reduction when necessary for safety.

questions.question: What is preserved by submuscular plating?
questions.answer: Muscle attachment, periosteal blood supply, fracture hematoma, and intermediate-fragment biology.

questions.question: Which window is common for a distal-third fracture?
questions.answer: A distal lateral window near the lateral femoral epicondyle.

questions.question: What alignment error particularly requires active assessment?
questions.answer: Femoral rotation, which can appear acceptable on limited fluoroscopic views.

approaches.name: Pediatric femoral-shaft safe zones for external-fixator pins
aliases: pediatric femoral external fixation safe zones
approaches.corridor: Anterolateral or direct-lateral percutaneous sleeves to bone, with level-specific trajectories and distal pins at least 2 cm proximal to the growth plate

sources.title: External fixation of femoral shaft fractures in children: enhanced stability with the use of an auxiliary pin
Treatment options in pediatric femoral shaft fractures

procedure_applications.condition: Temporary or definitive pediatric femoral external fixation is required and pins must preserve growth plates, neurovascular structures, joints, and future definitive fixation corridors

positioning.text: Position supine with the full thigh accessible, the hip and knee freely assessable, and fluoroscopy available for the femur and growth plates.

setup.text: Map the soft-tissue injury, physes, fracture, future nail or plate path, and pin-spread requirements before inserting any pin.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the greater trochanter and its lateral face, vastus lateralis, rectus-vastus interval, lateral epicondyle, distal femoral growth plate, and intended definitive incisions.

incision.text: Use an adequate stab incision at each planned anterolateral or direct-lateral site and bluntly spread through soft tissue to bone before placing the sleeve.

superficial_interval.text: Pass proximally through vastus lateralis, at midshaft directly lateral or between rectus femoris and vastus lateralis, and distally avoid tethering the inferior vastus-lateralis border.

deep_interval.text: Advance with a protected sleeve to lateral cortex, obtain controlled bicortical purchase, and stop before medial overpenetration.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, fascia, vastus-lateralis or rectus-vastus corridor, thick periosteum, lateral cortex, canal, then controlled far-cortex purchase.

structures_encountered.text: Circumferential thigh muscle, vastus lateralis, rectus femoris, greater trochanter, femoral periosteum, shaft cortex, and distal physis define pin placement.

structures_at_risk.text: Medial femoral neurovascular structures, sciatic nerve posteriorly, distal growth plate, knee capsule, muscle and skin, and future fixation corridors are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Avoid medial cortical plunge, posterior trajectories, injured skin, transphyseal or intracapsular pins, and distal pins closer than 2 cm to the growth plate.

retraction_hazards.text: Release tethered skin and muscle around each pin, cool drilling to limit thermal injury, and avoid forcing a sleeve through tense soft tissue.

exposure.text: Provides safe skeletal purchase for temporary damage-control or selected definitive external fixation with minimal surgical exposure.

limitations.text: Safe zones are guides rather than substitutes for patient-specific imaging; external fixation carries pin-track, alignment, and refracture concerns.

extensions.text: Add or relocate a pin only after remapping physes, neurovascular anatomy, soft tissue, and planned definitive fixation; increase spread without entering joints or growth plates.

indications.text: Use for damage-control stabilization, severe soft-tissue injury, polytrauma, unstable reduction, or selected definitive pediatric shaft fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid infected or severely damaged pin sites, corridors conflicting with definitive fixation, uncertain physeal location, and anatomy that cannot be safely localized.

implant_implications.text: Maximize safe pin spread and bicortical purchase, keep pins outside future nail and plate paths, and add stability without sacrificing physeal or neurovascular safety.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm trajectory, bicortical depth without medial overpenetration, fracture distance, joint clearance, and at least 2-cm distal physeal clearance on orthogonal views.

closure.text: Release soft-tissue tethering, dress pin sites, document distal perfusion and nerve function, and reassess hip and knee motion after frame assembly.

complications.text: Complications include neurovascular injury, physeal injury, pin-track infection, thermal necrosis, muscle tethering, loss of reduction, malunion, knee stiffness, and refracture after removal.

bailouts.text: If trajectory or physis is uncertain, stop drilling and relocate under imaging; for medial plunge or vascular concern, leave a tamponading pin in place and obtain urgent vascular assessment rather than blind removal.

questions.question: What are the safest general femoral pin regions?
How close may a distal pin be to the physis?
questions.answer: It should remain at least 2 cm proximal.

questions.question: Why avoid medial overpenetration?
questions.answer: The major femoral neurovascular structures lie medially and can be injured by drill or pin plunge.
